new_entities.name: Artificial food dyes
new_entities.description: Synthetic food coloring additives consumed in foods and beverages.

new_entities.name: ADHD symptoms in children
new_entities.description: Hyperactivity, impulsivity, and attention-related symptoms in children.

edges.effect_quant: A 2004 meta-analysis of 15 double-blind placebo-controlled trials estimated an overall effect size of 0.283 for artificial food colorings on hyperactivity symptoms, and a 2011 updated meta-analysis concluded that synthetic food colors may contribute to ADHD symptoms in a susceptible subgroup, although the overall effect remained modest and heterogeneous.
edges.population: children with ADHD, hyperactive syndromes, or suspected food-color sensitivity
edges.mechanism: Some children may have neurobehavioral sensitivity to certain food additives, but the response is inconsistent and likely limited to susceptible subgroups rather than the general child population.
edges.summary: Artificial food dyes deserve a mixed rather than dismissive verdict. The pooled literature suggests a modest average effect with probable responder subgroups, but the signal is not strong or consistent enough to frame dyes as a universal major driver of childhood ADHD symptoms.
edges.caveats: Do not oversell elimination diets as a standalone ADHD treatment. The most accurate framing is that dyes may worsen symptoms in some children, while many others show little or no measurable response.

evidence.citation: Schab DW et al 2004 J Dev Behav Pediatr
evidence.notes: Do artificial food colors promote hyperactivity in children with hyperactive syndromes? A meta-analysis of double-blind placebo-controlled trials.

evidence.citation: Nigg JT et al 2012 J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
evidence.notes: Meta-analysis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms, restriction diet, and synthetic food color additives.

evidence.citation: Rowe KS et al 1994 J Paediatr Child Health
evidence.notes: Synthetic food coloring and behavior: a dose response effect in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, repeated-measures study.
